newsitem.title: USA: Reinhard gets a break, wins big McDonald's task.
newsitem.headline: Reinhard gets a break, wins big McDonald's task.

text.p: Keith Reinhard, chairman and chief executive of DDB Needham Worldwide and creator of the famous McDonald's theme "You deserve a break today," got a big break Tuesday.

The agency's Chicago office, a unit of Omnicom Group, on Tuesday won back the lead position on the fast-food giant's $600 million advertising account from crosstown rival Leo Burnett Co. The high-stakes competition had been closely watched in the advertising industry.
Needham, which already had a portion of McDonald's business, is now responsible for all adult and promotion advertising activity for the Oak Brook, Ill.-based hamburger chain.

Leo Burnett, which had the lead position on McDonald's business for more than 15 years, will now handle kids, pre-teens and Ronald McDonald advertising domestically. No changes have been made in McDonald's regional and speciality advertising.
Reinhard, who worked on McDonald's while at Needham's Chicago office, has been gunning for the McDonald's business ever since the agency lost the lead position to Burnett in 1981.

"There is something about your first love," he said in a telephone interview after the announcement. "McDonald's was in many ways that for me as a creative. It was the first really big campaign I was involved with."
In addition to the "You deserve a break today" slogan, Reinhard went on to work on the "Two all-beef patties" slogan as well as helping to invent the "McDonald Land" characters.
After his agency lost the lead portion of the business, DDB Needham continued work for the client internationally, doing work on McDonald's advertising in 45 countries, Reinhard said.
"To win back the lead agency status in the U.S., the home market where it all began, is pretty special," he said.
With the changes, Needham will be responsible for all adult and promotion advertising activity as well as overall brand positioning and creative direction. New advertising is expected by Sept. 1.
Though DDB Needham's Reinhard got his break, Burnett, which has suffered a string of high-profile creative losses this year, can't seem to get one.
For many years, Burnett led what some industry observers called a charmed existence.
"It seemed like business came in over their transom," one Chicago agency observer said.

But trouble began hovering over the agency last fall when the agency lost the $100 million United Airlines account after 31 years. In December, it lost the $85 million creative portion of the Miller Lite business. In March, Burnett forced out two top executives. In May, it resigned the $65 million Reebok business.
"I think that Burnett has experienced a situation that is endemic to our industry," a Burnett spokesman said, referring to the client defections.

Some industry observers said they believed McDonald's was using Burnett as a scapegoat for its recently failed Campaign 55 national promotion, which some franchisees said failed to drive sales at lunch and dinner. Burnett created the advertising campaign, themed "My McDonald's," which supported that promotion.
"Burnett got caught in the domestic problems McDonald's is having currently," said Ron Paul, president of Technomic Inc., a Chicago-based restaurant consulting firm.
Others suggested that McDonald's is using the shift in advertising agencies to show that it is attempting to address problems with its core business.

"I think McDonald's is confusing motion with movement," said Dennis Jorgensen, chief executive officer of the American Marketing Association. "I think they need to effectively deal with value, quick (service) and taste. None of those things has anything to do with advertising."
Despite the losses, Burnett has managed to win new business this year from such blue-chip clients as Procter & Gamble Co., Coca-Cola Co., Walgreen Co. and Eli Lilly Co.

"We've still gotten over half a billion dollars in new billings in the U.S. alone over the past 18 months," a Burnett spokesman said. "We continue to handle five of the world's seven largest brands. We handle seven of the nation's top 20 brands. The foundation of this company continues to be rock solid from a financial standpoint," he said.

For Burnett, the challenge will be to turn around the perception that it is on a losing streak, said Jack Trout, president of Trout & Partners, a Greenwich, Conn. marketing strategy firm. "That isn't easy."
